About the app

What is Goodreads?

01

Goodreads is the largest social cataloguing platform for readers: a place to log books read, rate and review them, follow friends, and get recommendations. Launched in 2007 and acquired by Amazon in 2013, it has grown into the default “reading resume” for millions of book lovers, even as its interface has stayed largely unchanged for over a decade.

Key findings

Simplified navigation

Make the app structure clearer and reduce the effort required to access important features.

Better book discovery

Improve search and browsing so users can find relevant books more easily.

Personalised recommendations

Use reading preferences and behaviour to give more relevant recommendations and reduce decision fatigue.

Improved social interaction

Make reviews, ratings, discussions and sharing easier to discover and interact with.

Better reading management

Make reading lists, shelves, progress and tracking more organised and intuitive.

Accessible interface

Follow WCAG 2.2 through readable typography, sufficient colour contrast, clear labels, consistent navigation and accessible interactions.

User interviews

Five readers,
in their own words

Ten-minute semi-structured conversations with the same six prompts and open follow-ups, chosen to span avid daily readers to people who've never opened the app. Tap a card to see what each one needs.

06

Merin's profile is hypothetical, so her needs are treated as a design hypothesis rather than a confirmed interview finding.

Simple navigation matters

Participants preferred a balance of features and simplicity. Difficult navigation and hidden functions make basic actions harder to access.

Discovery needs more context

Descriptions, genres, ratings and personalised recommendations help readers decide which books to explore, rather than relying on a title alone.

Effortless library management

Wishlists, book scanning, reading shelves and easy access to saved books support how readers organise their reading.

Different review perspectives

Readers want recent, negative and varied reviews, not just an overall rating, when evaluating a book.

Pain points & insights

Eight problems
on the shelf

Each one triangulated across secondary research, survey data and interviews. Pull a book off the shelf.

07
1

Readers demand minimalist, high-hierarchy interfaces

Across the survey, interviews and secondary research, the loudest signal is a demand for restraint: fewer competing elements, a clear reading order, and covers doing more of the communicating than text.

78.2%rate readability as highly important (4–5 of 5)
41.3%prefer a grid of book covers over lists or text
2

Trust is earned through personal relevance, not popularity

Popular lists and star ratings aren't enough. Readers respond better to recommendations based on what they've read, liked, or are in the mood for.

28.3%trust recommendations based on their own reading
2.2%trust “popular / trending” books alone
3

An awareness-to-usage gap, not a brand problem

Goodreads is well known, but usability holds it back. 81.3% of users struggled to find features, and icon and label clarity scored only 2.9/5.

69.6%recognise the Goodreads brand
21.7%actually use it actively today
4

Consistency & clarity build a smoother reading experience

Readers need an interface that feels predictable, readable and easy to understand on every page. Consistent layouts, clearer interactions and better feedback reduce confusion.

78.2%rate readability as highly important
75%report difficulty finding or navigating certain features

Conclusion

Design priorities
for the redesign

10

Simplify the book detail page

Prioritise the essentials: cover, title, author, rating and a short description. Move secondary metadata, links and promotional content lower.

Make discovery visual & personal

A visual grid of book covers, with recommendations built around mood, genre, reading history and interests rather than popularity.

Simplify navigation & search

Make the most-used features easy to reach, improve search, cut unnecessary steps and create a clearer, more predictable structure.

Give users more control

Let readers customise their home, organise shelves, filter reviews and choose how information is displayed.

Create a low-pressure onboarding

Start with a few simple preferences and offer relevant recommendations immediately, before asking for more.

Improve consistency & everyday usability

One visual system across pages and devices, fixing frequent small frustrations like readability, dark mode and unclear interactions.
